edges.relationship: Philip J. Deloria draws on Wilson’s account of oral tradition’s contextual rules and review by knowledgeable audiences when explaining its historical legitimacy (2002).
edges.evidence_note: A specifically credited methodological resource in Deloria’s own chapter, not a claim of personal mentoring or a general career lineage. He cites Wilson’s 1997 essay, whose body remains unread here; the 1996 essay is a distinct work.

edges.relationship: Deloria identifies a tension in Wilson’s oral-history argument between shared practices for checking accuracy and an epistemology that challenges Western historical knowledge (2002).
edges.evidence_note: Qualified methodological reception within his recognition of Native historical authority. His characterization of purity and difference is attributed to him; it does not replace Wilson’s own situated family/community claims or her recorded acknowledgment of archival scholarship’s value and limits.

edges.relationship: As Gonzalez, Modzelewski, Panich and Schneider explain, Wilson credits Fanon’s writing on decolonization with helping her articulate her own struggle in Reclaiming Our Humanity (2004).
edges.evidence_note: Explicitly mediated through the four named authors’ substantive 2006 account, read in an institutional repository. They also credit Paulo Freire’s work on praxis; his contribution is not reassigned to Fanon. Wilson’s original 2004 chapter remains unread here, and her family and community sources of knowledge retain their independent standing.

edges.relationship: Deloria criticized the culturally biased social-scientific approach of the workshops McNickle organized, as David Beck’s 1995 history reports.
edges.evidence_note: Program-level criticism, not rejection of all McNickle’s writing. Beck identifies Deloria as a guest speaker at the 1965 workshop and one of its critics, citing Dorothy Parker (1992), p. 195; that book and Deloria’s original statement remain unread. Douglas Miller’s 2016 review separately describes a widening ideological gulf, while challenging a dismissive account of McNickle. Neither source establishes McNickle as Deloria’s mentor.

edges.relationship: Wheeler uses Ahenakew’s written Old Keyam narrative to show why interpreting recorded Cree knowledge requires its language, relationships and cultural contexts (2018).
edges.evidence_note: A situated resource for oral-history interpretation, not a claim that Ahenakew founded the modern field. Wheeler credits Maria Campbell’s interpretation of coded teachings; Campbell’s unpublished 1999 paper is unread. Thunderchild’s narration, Ahenakew’s writing and Ruth Buck’s later editing remain distinct.

edges.relationship: In her 2003 review, Beatrice Medicine identifies Ahenakew among the Indigenous scholars whose historical insights inform Carter’s 1999 survey.
edges.evidence_note: Explicitly attributed scholarly review of Aboriginal People and Colonizers of Western Canada to 1900; the book body remains unread. This records reported use of historical insight, not mentorship, exclusive influence or a verified particular Ahenakew work. Medicine’s Big Bear example and Christine Welsh’s formulation are not assigned to Ahenakew.

edges.relationship: Adams criticizes Sioui’s emphasis on guilt and moral reconciliation for inadequately addressing the economic and political structures of colonial domination (1992).
edges.evidence_note: A specific argument in Adams’s review of the English translation, credited to Sheila Fischman. He also finds the Sacred Circle discussion useful. The atlas records his criticism without adopting his separate epidemiological assertions or his judgment of who possesses an Aboriginal consciousness; Sioui’s whole book remains unread.

edges.relationship: Dickason questions Sioui’s presentation of Lahontan as the first European to appreciate Indigenous thought, pointing to the earlier Las Casas while urging respectful attention to Sioui’s argument (1992).
edges.evidence_note: The review discusses both Trigger and Sioui; only its Sioui-specific passage supports this relationship. This is a bounded correction within an appreciative reception, not wholesale rejection of autohistory. The reviewed French original is dated 1989; the English translation is a separate 1992 manifestation.

edges.relationship: Sioui recalls that Lévi-Strauss read and endorsed his work after Pierre Maranda passed it on, providing encouragement during his return to university.
edges.evidence_note: Reported in Sioui’s 2013 interview with Katie Hyslop. Maranda retains the mediating role; the underlying letter or manuscript was not obtained, and the recollection does not establish formal supervision, structuralist influence, or endorsement of every historical claim. No precise date for the earlier exchange is invented.

edges.relationship: As Deborah Simmons interprets his work, Adams draws on Fanon’s account of decolonization to connect autobiographical experiences of colonial alienation with collective historical struggle.
edges.evidence_note: Explicitly mediated through Simmons’s 2002 tribute, pp. 6–7. Her reading connects Prison of Grass and Tortured People; their original and revised editions remain distinct. This is a specified intellectual resource, not an inference from Adams’s Marxist politics. The complete book bodies remain unread here.

edges.relationship: Palmer uses Adams’s criticism of state-funded Indigenous leadership to develop his history of the linked struggles against capitalism and colonialism (2024).
edges.evidence_note: A specifically used historical argument, not personal mentoring or wholesale endorsement. Palmer distinguishes Adams’s position from Harold Cardinal’s and also qualifies Adams’s overincarceration figures. The selected Palmer passages were freshly read; Adams’s cited book passages were not independently checked in their entirety.
